strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: attached shadow detection, distinct from the well-studied cast shadow detection task, with clear motivation and physical grounding (surface normal · light direction relationship).

Introduces a new dataset (1,458 images) with separate cast/attached shadow annotations, plus normal maps and heuristic 3D light directions, sourced and curated from three existing datasets (WSRD, SOBA, CUHK) — a useful resource for the community even though it is modestly sized.

The proposed closed-loop iterative framework linking shadow detection and light estimation is intuitive and physically motivated, unifying classical illumination-geometry reasoning with modern deep learning.

Thorough ablation studies (surface normal guidance, iterative refinement depth, individual loss terms) that support each design choice, and reasonable analysis of diminishing/negative returns beyond 3 iterations.

Strong quantitative improvements specifically for attached shadow detection (>33% BER reduction) while maintaining competitive cast/full shadow performance, with qualitative examples showing geometry-consistent shadow boundaries versus baselines that mostly capture appearance-based cues.
Honest limitations section discussing dependence on off-the-shelf normal estimation, lack of instance-level cast-attached association, and the single directional light assumption.
weaknesses: The dataset is relatively small (1,166 train / 292 test) and derived largely by re-annotating/relabeling existing datasets (WSRD, SOBA, CUHK) rather than fully new captures; the heuristic light-direction estimation for SOBA/CUHK (derived from object-shadow centroid displacement and relative depth) is itself an approximate, non-ground-truth signal, which could introduce label noise/bias to both the light supervision and the geometry-based partial shadow maps used for training and evaluation.

The reliance on a monocular depth/normal estimation foundation model (Depth Anything v2) introduces a strong dependency on that model's accuracy; the paper's own limitation figure shows failure cases from inaccurate normals, but there's no quantitative sensitivity analysis of how normal-map quality propagates to final shadow/light accuracy.

The single directional-light assumption is a significant simplification that limits applicability to many real-world scenes (multiple lights, area lights, indoor/night scenes), and this is acknowledged only qualitatively without any quantitative evaluation on multi-light scenarios.

Comparison baselines are original shadow detectors not designed for this task and are only partially retrained (some evaluated purely on SBU-pretrained weights), making the 'cast-focused' baselines' underperformance on attached shadows somewhat unsurprising rather than a fully fair apples-to-apples comparison; only 4 of 7 baselines were retrained on the new dataset.

No explicit mechanism ties detected cast shadows to their corresponding attached shadows per-instance, which is acknowledged as a limitation but could meaningfully affect the practical utility of the method in multi-object scenes.

The paper lacks error bars, statistical significance testing, or multiple-seed results, and does not report failure-case statistics beyond a few illustrative examples, making it hard to assess robustness across the diverse scene types in the dataset.

Cast shadow BER is only 'comparable' to prior methods rather than improved, and improvements are not uniformly dominant across all metrics (e.g., SILT† has better cast BER), so the overall gains, while real for attached shadows, are somewhat narrower for the cast/full shadow tasks.

strengths: Identifies and addresses a genuinely under-studied problem: separating attached shadows from cast shadows, which prior benchmarks largely conflate or ignore.

Introduces a new dataset with explicit cast/attached shadow separation, aggregated from three existing sources (WSRD, SOBA, CUHK) with normal maps and heuristic light directions — a potentially useful resource for future work if released.
The core idea of coupling light estimation and geometry-derived partial shadow maps in a closed feedback loop is conceptually appealing and grounded in classical illumination-shadow reasoning.
Reasonably thorough ablations (normal guidance, number of iterations, individual loss terms) that support the claimed design choices.

Substantial and consistent improvement on attached-shadow BER (>33% relative) over multiple retrained/pretrained baselines, with qualitative examples showing better geometric consistency than appearance-based baselines.
weaknesses: The 'physics-grounded' claim is undercut by the crude approximation used: attached shadow prediction relies solely on a per-pixel dot product n·ℓ>0 with no visibility, ray-tracing, or self-occlusion reasoning, and the underlying normals come from a monocular relative-depth model rather than accurate geometry, so both inputs to the 'physical' model are approximate — this is acknowledged as a limitation but is fairly central to the paper's core claim.

Dataset is small (1,458 images total, 292 test) relative to existing cast-shadow benchmarks (SBU 4.1K, ViSha 11.7K, CUHK 10.5K), which limits statistical confidence in the reported gains and raises questions about generalization.

Ground-truth light directions for 2 of the 3 constituent datasets (SOBA, CUHK) are themselves heuristically derived (from object/shadow centroid displacement and relative depth), not measured — using estimated 'ground truth' to both supervise and evaluate the light estimation module raises circularity/reliability concerns that are not discussed.

No explicit quantitative evaluation of light-direction estimation accuracy (e.g., angular error) is reported in the main text, despite light estimation being one of the two core modules; only indirect evidence via shadow-metric ablations is given.

Cast shadow BER is not improved over baselines (e.g., SILT retrained achieves 4.52 vs. the proposed method's 5.04), so the gains are essentially confined to the attached-shadow category while cast performance is only 'comparable,' weakening the claim of a unified improvement across both shadow types.

The single-directional-light assumption is a significant simplification for real-world scenes with multiple/ambient light sources (explicitly acknowledged as a limitation but still limits applicability to outdoor single-object scenarios shown in the qualitative figures).

The evaluation protocol for baselines (splitting a single predicted shadow mask into cast/attached post-hoc using object masks) is not necessarily a fair comparison, since none of these baselines were designed or trained to separate the two shadow types, potentially inflating the apparent advantage of the proposed method beyond what the underlying detection quality would justify.

Technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the shadow detector reuses the SILT backbone, the light module is a standard ConvNeXt-S, and the light-direction parameterization is adopted directly from prior work; the primary novel contributions are the iterative feedback scheme and loss design, which are relatively simple engineering additions rather than fundamentally new modeling.

The paper does not compare quantitatively against the classical joint shadow-illumination-geometry approach it repeatedly cites (Panagopoulos et al.), leaving the claimed advance over 'classical illumination reasoning' unsubstantiated empirically.

strengths: Identifies and addresses a genuine, under-explored gap in shadow detection literature: the lack of dedicated methods and datasets for attached (self-occlusion) shadows, as distinguished from cast shadows.

The physics-grounded closed-loop design linking shadow detection and light estimation via surface normals is intuitive and well-motivated, unifying classical illumination reasoning with modern deep learning.

Introduces a new annotated dataset (1,458 images, cast/attached split, sourced from WSRD, SOBA, CUHK) that fills a clear gap in existing benchmarks (Table 1 comparison is convincing) and should be useful to the community.

Strong quantitative improvements on attached shadow detection (at least 33% BER reduction) while maintaining competitive full and cast shadow performance, evaluated against seven baselines including retrained variants on the new dataset.
Reasonably thorough ablations (geometry guidance, iterative refinement depth, individual loss terms) that support the design choices and show each component's contribution.
Qualitative results (Fig. 5, 6) illustrate physically sensible predictions and an interesting generalization capability where the model predicts shadows outside the annotated foreground regions.
Limitations section is candid about dependency on normal-map quality, lack of per-instance cast-attached association, and the single-directional-light assumption.
weaknesses: The dataset is derived in part from heuristic/pseudo light-direction annotations (SOBA/CUHK) computed from 2D object-to-shadow centroid displacement and relative depth rather than ground-truth measurements, which could introduce systematic noise into both training supervision and evaluation of the light estimation module; no assessment of this heuristic's accuracy is provided.

Normal maps used for both training and dataset construction are generated by an off-the-shelf monocular depth-to-normal model rather than measured geometry, so both the 'geometry' partial map and part of the ground-truth pipeline rely on approximate/noisy pseudo-labels; the paper acknowledges this only as a limitation without quantifying its impact.

The assumption of a single global directional light is a significant simplification not well suited to many real-world/indoor/multi-source scenes, and the dataset itself may not adequately represent such conditions, limiting claimed generality.

Dataset size (1,458 images, 292 test) is relatively small compared to existing shadow detection benchmarks (e.g., ViSha 11.7K, CUHK 10.5K), which may limit statistical robustness of the reported gains and generalization claims.

No explicit computational/parameter comparison against baselines is given beyond a brief inference-time note (0.18s vs 0.55s for iterations); it's unclear how much extra cost the dual-module iterative architecture adds relative to single-pass baselines overall.
Cast shadow BER is only 'comparable' to prior methods (Table 2 shows SILT retrained achieves lower cast BER 4.52 vs. Ours 5.04), suggesting a trade-off that is not deeply analyzed or discussed.

The paper does not report inter-annotator agreement or annotation quality control for the manually labeled cast/attached masks, which affects reproducibility and confidence in the benchmark's reliability.

No explicit discussion of failure cases beyond Fig. 8, and no error bars/multiple-run variance are reported for the main quantitative results, making it hard to judge significance of the improvements.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: joint detection of cast and attached shadows with an explicit distinction, motivated by a clear physical intuition (surfaces facing away from light fall into shadow).

The iterative feedback loop between light estimation and shadow detection is a sensible, well-motivated architectural choice, and the ablations (Table 3, Fig. 7) convincingly show that both the geometry prior (normal maps) and the iterative refinement contribute measurable gains, with performance saturating after ~3 iterations.

Introduces a new curated dataset (1,458 images from WSRD/SOBA/CUHK) with separate cast/attached/undefined annotations, filling a real gap identified in Table 1; this could be a useful resource for the community regardless of the specific method proposed.

Quantitative results show large improvements on attached-shadow BER (>33% reduction over retrained baselines) while maintaining competitive full/cast performance, and the qualitative figures (Fig. 5, Fig. 7 main text, Figs. 5-9 supplementary) support the claim that geometry/lighting cues yield more physically consistent attached-shadow boundaries than appearance-only baselines.

Reasonable additional validation: standalone light-estimation upper bound analysis, cross-dataset qualitative generalization (SRD, SBU-TimeLapse, ViSha), a downstream shadow-removal application with a user study, and computational overhead reporting, which together give a fairly complete picture of the method's behavior and cost.
weaknesses: The dataset's 'ground truth' for light direction and, indirectly, attached-shadow masks is itself heuristic for two of the three sources (SOBA, CUHK): light directions are derived from object/cast-shadow centroids and coarse relative depth, and attached-shadow masks were initialized from a geometry+light-derived prior mask before manual correction. Since the proposed method also reasons via geometry+light, there is a risk of annotation-model correlation biasing evaluation in the method's favor; only WSRD (42 test images) has calibrated, independent light-direction ground truth.

Cast-shadow BER is only 'comparable' to prior methods rather than improved, and the overall framework's main gains are concentrated in the attached and full-shadow metrics; this should be discussed more explicitly as a trade-off rather than folded into an overall 'outperforms' narrative.

Cross-dataset generalization (SRD, SBU-TimeLapse, ViSha) is evaluated only qualitatively with no quantitative metrics, so claims of robustness to unseen domains/temporal shadow variation are not rigorously substantiated.

The 'undefined shadow' regions (pixels not attributable to annotated foreground objects) are excluded from cast/attached training and evaluation; this may remove some of the harder or more ambiguous cases from the benchmark, potentially inflating reported cast/attached numbers relative to a full-scene evaluation.

Test set is small (292 images across 3 heterogeneous sources) with no reported variance across seeds/splits, making it hard to assess the statistical robustness of the reported gains, especially the fairly small margins on cast metrics.

Method relies on off-the-shelf monocular depth/normal estimation and a single dominant directional light assumption; both are acknowledged as limitations, but this considerably narrows applicability to outdoor/single-light scenes and makes performance sensitive to upstream normal-estimation errors, as shown in the authors' own limitation figure.

The iterative design roughly triples inference time (0.545s vs 0.176s per image) and training requires two GPUs versus a single GPU for baselines, which is a non-trivial cost not fully contextualized against the modest additional gains beyond 2 iterations.

strengths: Addresses an underexplored and well-motivated problem: most shadow detectors predict a single unified mask or ignore attached shadows entirely, and the paper gives a clear physical rationale (surfaces facing away from the light fall into shadow) for jointly modeling cast and attached shadows.

Contributes a new, carefully curated dataset (1,458 images from WSRD/SOBA/CUHK) with separate cast/attached/undefined shadow annotations, normal maps, and light directions, including documented manual correction procedures (Figs. 10-12) that could be useful to the community.

The iterative dual-module design (shadow detector <-> light estimator) is intuitively coupled to the physics of shadow formation, and the ablations (Table 3/Table 1 in supp.) reasonably isolate the contributions of surface normals, number of iterations, and individual loss terms.

Fairly extensive empirical validation: comparisons against 7 baselines (with and without fine-tuning), cross-dataset qualitative generalization on SBU-TimeLapse, ViSha, and SRD, a downstream shadow-removal application with a user study, and supplementary reporting of computational overhead and standalone light-estimation accuracy.

Reported quantitative gains are sizable (>=33% attached-shadow BER reduction) and consistent across full/cast/attached metrics, and qualitative figures visibly show better attached-shadow boundaries than baselines that rely purely on appearance cues.
weaknesses: The method's physical grounding rests on weak proxies: for SOBA/CUHK (the majority of the dataset), the "ground-truth" light direction used for supervision is itself a heuristic computed from object/cast-shadow centroid displacement and coarse monocular depth differences, not a measured or calibrated quantity. This creates circularity — the light-estimation loss is trained to match a heuristic rather than true geometry, which undercuts the claimed physical rigor, and light-direction accuracy is only quantitatively validated on 42 WSRD images with true calibration.

Surface normals, central to the "geometry-aware" claim, are derived in a very simplified way (z=1, x/y from image-plane depth gradients of a monocular relative-depth estimate), rather than from a dedicated normal predictor or real 3D sensing. The paper's own limitations section acknowledges this propagates errors into predictions (Fig. 10), which is a substantive caveat given normals are the core geometric cue.

The curated dataset, while valuable, is modest in size (1,166 train / 292 test) and derived entirely from existing datasets with heuristic/manual relabeling rather than independently verified ground truth; evaluation of cast/attached separation explicitly excludes "undefined" shadow pixels, which could inflate apparent performance relative to a setting with full dense labels.

Baseline comparisons are restricted to relatively dated cast-shadow-focused detectors (BDRAR 2018, DSD, FSDNet, MTMT, FDRNet, SDCM, SILT); more recent transformer/diffusion-based or object-centric methods mentioned in related work (e.g., SwinShadow, MetaShadow) are not empirically compared, leaving the relative advantage over current SOTA less certain.

The shadow-removal application is evaluated only via a subjective user-preference study (no shadow-free ground truth, no quantitative removal metrics such as RMSE/PSNR), which weakens the strength of the downstream-utility claim despite being a reasonable workaround given data constraints.

The approach assumes a single global directional light source, which the authors acknowledge limits applicability to multi-source, soft-shadow, or low-light scenes — a meaningful restriction for real-world generality, though appropriately disclosed as a limitation.

Practical overhead is non-trivial: the full iterative model requires two GPUs for training and is ~3x slower at inference than a non-iterative variant (0.545s vs 0.18s per image), which may limit applicability in latency-sensitive settings; this trade-off is reported but not deeply analyzed against the accuracy gain from 2 to 3 iterations, which is fairly marginal.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely under-explored problem: most prior shadow detectors output a single unified mask or ignore attached shadows entirely; this paper explicitly separates cast and attached shadows and grounds the separation in a physical model relating surface normals and light direction.

The iterative closed-loop design (shadow detection <-> light estimation) is well motivated and clearly explained, with a geometry-derived partial attached-shadow map used as an interpretable intermediate signal that is fed back into the detector.

Contributes a new curated dataset (1,458 images) built from three existing benchmarks (WSRD, SOBA, CUHK) with explicit, manually corrected cast/attached/undefined annotations, normal maps, and light directions — a useful resource for future work in this under-annotated area.

Strong empirical results: consistent improvement on full and attached-shadow BER/F1 versus 7 competitive baselines (including retrained variants), with at least 33% reduction in attached BER while maintaining competitive cast performance.

Comprehensive ablations isolate the contribution of surface-normal guidance, number of refinement iterations, and each individual loss term, and results are consistent with the paper's stated claims (geometry provides the largest single gain; iterations saturate around 3).

Practical downstream validation via shadow removal with a human preference study (80.7% prefer separate attached/cast refinement), plus cross-dataset qualitative generalization to SRD, SBU-TimeLapse, and ViSha, supporting real-world usefulness beyond the curated benchmark.

Limitations (dependence on off-the-shelf normal estimation, single-directional-light assumption) are explicitly and honestly discussed rather than omitted, and the supplementary material provides substantial additional detail on dataset construction, architecture, and inference overhead, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Ground-truth light directions for SOBA and CUHK are only heuristic estimates derived from object/shadow centroid displacement and coarse depth difference, not verified real light directions; this introduces label noise into both training supervision and quantitative light-direction evaluation (only WSRD has calibrated ground truth, and light-direction accuracy is validated on just 42 test images).

The method's cast-shadow BER (5.04) is not actually better than the best prior fine-tuned baseline (SILT: 4.52), and the paper's own text concedes cast BER is merely "comparable," so the claimed overall superiority rests mainly on attached and full-shadow metrics.

The geometric priors (surface normals) are derived from an off-the-shelf monocular depth model, and the paper acknowledges predictions degrade when these normals are inaccurate (Fig. 10); no quantitative sensitivity analysis of performance versus normal-estimation quality is provided.

Single dominant directional light assumption limits applicability to multi-light, indoor, or diffuse/soft-shadow scenes, which the authors note but do not empirically probe (e.g., no evaluation on an indoor or multi-light benchmark).

Architectural novelty is somewhat incremental: the shadow-detection backbone reuses SILT with additional input channels, and the light estimator reuses ConvNeXt-S; the core contribution is the iterative feedback scheme and multi-task losses rather than a fundamentally new architecture.

Iterative inference adds meaningful computational cost (0.545s vs 0.176s non-iterative per image, and training requires 2 GPUs vs 1 for baselines), which is disclosed but not deeply analyzed in terms of accuracy/efficiency trade-offs beyond the ablation table.

Annotation quality for the new dataset relies on manual correction of heuristic/model-derived masks without reported inter-annotator agreement or annotation protocol validation, leaving some uncertainty about label reliability, especially for the excluded "undefined" shadow regions which could bias cast/attached metrics by removing ambiguous, harder pixels from evaluation.
